verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A identifies a specific EU aviation-security regulation (Regulation (EC) No 300/2008). Definition B identifies the security of network and information systems by reference to Article 6(2) of Directive (EU) 2022/2555. One is a legal instrument citation concerning civil aviation security; the other is a substantive cybersecurity concept.
verdict.evidence_span_a: verordening (eg) nr. 300/2008 van het europees parlement en de raad van 11 maart 2008 inzake gemeenschappelijke regels op het gebied van de beveiliging van de burgerluchtvaart en tot intrekking van verordening (eg) nr. 2320/2002(pbeu 2008, l 97);
verdict.evidence_span_b: beveiliging van netwerk- en informatiesystemen in de zin van artikel 6, punt 2, van richtlijn (eu) 2022/2555 ;

verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A describes a security property or capability of network and information systems: their ability to resist harmful events at a certain reliability level. Definition B describes a near-incident: a potentially harmful event that was successfully prevented or did not occur. They concern related security subject matter but are not the same concept; one is a system state/capability and the other is an event or prevented event.
verdict.practical_consequence: The same real-world situation could implicate both concepts but be classified differently: a system may possess or lack the defined security capability, while a prevented attempted disruption may qualify as a near-incident even if no loss of availability, authenticity, integrity, or confidentiality occurred. Treating them as interchangeable could duplicate or misallocate accountability between ongoing security obligations and incident reporting or response duties.
verdict.evidence_span_a: het vermogen van netwerk- en informatiesystemen om op een bepaald niveau van betrouwbaarheid weerstand te bieden aan elke gebeurtenis die de beschikbaarheid, authenticiteit, integriteit of vertrouwelijkheid van opgeslagen, verzonden of verwerkte gegevens of van de diensten die door of via deze netwerk- en informatiesystemen worden aangeboden, in gevaar kan brengen;
verdict.evidence_span_b: een gebeurtenis die de beschikbaarheid, authenticiteit, integriteit of vertrouwelijkheid van opgeslagen, verzonden of verwerkte gegevens of van de diensten die worden aangeboden door of toegankelijk zijn via netwerk- en informatiesystemen, in gevaar had kunnen brengen, maar die met succes is voorkomen of zich niet heeft voorgedaan;

verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A is an institutional and purpose-based category: electronic services provided by a Dutch administrative body or designated organization in connection with a public task, the public interest, or processing the citizen service number. Definition B is a cross-referenced, technology/market-based category whose scope is determined by the definition in Directive (EU) 2015/1535, rather than by the provider's public function or the specific public-interest/BSN conditions. A service can therefore fall within one definition but not the other, or fall within both for different reasons.
verdict.practical_consequence: The same provider or service could be subject to different regulatory classifications and obligations: a public authority's electronic service may be covered by Definition A even if it is not a 'digital service' under the cross-referenced EU definition, while a qualifying digital service supplied outside the public-task/BSN context may fall under Definition B but not Definition A. This can create inconsistent allocation of compliance and accountability responsibilities, including possible gaps or duplicated obligations where the regimes overlap.

verdict.evidence_span_b: een dienst zoals gedefinieerd in artikel 1, lid 1, punt b), van richtlijn (eu) 2015/1535 van het europees parlement en de raad (30);

verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A covers any natural or legal person carrying out an economic activity, regardless of legal form. Definition B covers a 'parent undertaking' by cross-reference to accounting-law provisions, which requires a parent/subsidiary or control relationship and is therefore a narrower, structurally defined category. A parent undertaking may fall within Definition A, but most undertakings under Definition A are not parent undertakings under Definition B.
verdict.practical_consequence: The same corporate group or undertaking could be an 'undertaking' for general economic-activity obligations under Instrument A but not a 'parent undertaking' for group-level or parent-specific obligations under Instrument B. Applying the wrong definition could create inconsistent classification or incorrectly assign, duplicate, or omit responsibility at parent versus subsidiary level.

verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A is a broad concept covering any natural or legal person carrying out an economic activity, regardless of legal form. Definition B is a sector-specific insurance undertaking defined by reference to Directive 2009/138/EC. An insurance undertaking will generally fall within the broad category in A, but most entities covered by A are not insurance undertakings under B.
verdict.practical_consequence: The same insurance-sector actor may be classified as an 'onderneming' for general purposes under Definition A but only as a 'verzekeringsonderneming' under the narrower sectoral regime in Definition B. Applying one definition in place of the other could improperly extend or omit sector-specific obligations, creating inconsistent classification and potentially duplicated or dropped responsibility.

verdict.evidence_span_b: andere gegevens dan persoonsgegevens zoals gedefinieerd in artikel 4, punt 1, van verordening (eu) 2016/679;

Definition B concerns high-impact capabilities of general-purpose AI models, benchmarked against the most advanced such models. They address different objects, criteria, and regulatory roles.

verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A covers any independent public authority established by a Member State under Article 51, whereas Definition B designates a European supervisory authority appointed under Article 31(1)(b) of the Regulation. Both concern supervisory authorities, but they differ in institutional level, legal basis, and designated role; the latter is specifically the lead overseer for the Regulation's purposes.
verdict.practical_consequence: The same supervised entity or activity could fall under a Member State supervisory authority under Definition A while having a different European authority designated as lead overseer under Definition B, creating potentially different supervisory responsibility or coordination obligations rather than a single interchangeable authority.
verdict.evidence_span_a: een door een lidstaat ingevolge artikel 51 ingestelde onafhankelijke overheidsinstantie;
verdict.evidence_span_b: de overeenkomstig artikel 31, lid 1, punt b), van deze verordening aangewezen europese toezichthoudende autoriteit;

verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A covers any potential circumstance, event, or action capable of harming or negatively affecting network and information systems, their users, or other persons. Definition B is a narrower, qualified subset: a cyber threat whose technical characteristics indicate that it may cause a serious ICT-related incident or a serious payment-related operational or security incident. Thus, the same threat may fall within the broad category of “cyberdreiging” under A without meeting the severity, technical-indication, or incident-type thresholds of “significante cyberdreiging” under B.
verdict.practical_consequence: A threat could trigger general cyber-threat-related duties or classification under Definition A but not the heightened significant-threat treatment under Definition B, creating a potential scope or accountability gap if responsibilities depend on the narrower classification.

verdict.mismatch_description: The definitions refer to different regulated service-provider categories. Definition A incorporates the eIDAS concept of a trust service provider, while Definition B incorporates the PSD2 concept of an account information service provider. They do not describe the same role or scope merely because both concern providers of digital services.

Definition B concerns a managed service provider that installs, manages, operates, or maintains ICT products or systems for a customer. verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A covers an entity providing managed ICT services involving installation, management, operation, or maintenance for a customer. Definition B covers the person or organization that develops or commissions development of an AI system or general-purpose AI model and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark. A managed-service provider may operate or maintain an AI system for a customer without being its developer, market provider, or deployer under its own name.
verdict.practical_consequence: The same real-world AI-related activity could be treated differently: a managed-service provider could bear responsibilities for operational ICT management under Definition A, while responsibility as the AI 'provider' under Definition B would remain with the developer or entity placing the system into service. Conversely, an entity performing both roles could have distinct and potentially cumulative obligations; treating the roles as identical could misassign or duplicate accountability.

Thus, an element may fall within the broader 'ict-product' concept without being a software or hardware asset used by a financial entity.
verdict.practical_consequence: The same technology or system component could be in scope under the broader product definition but outside the financial-entity asset definition, creating inconsistent classification and potentially leaving related accountability or compliance obligations unassigned under the narrower instrument.

verdict.mismatch_description: The definitions are cross-references to different provisions and use different legal categories: an 'essentiële entiteit' is an entity covered by articles 8–11, while an 'aangewezen organisatie' is an organization covered by article 2(2). Without the content of those referenced provisions, it cannot be established whether the categories overlap, coincide, or are unrelated in practice.

verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A concerns an unplanned cybersecurity event or linked events affecting network and information-system security, data properties, or services provided by a financial entity. Definition B concerns an incident or malfunction of an AI system that produces specified severe consequences, including death or serious health harm, critical-infrastructure disruption, or violation of fundamental-rights obligations. An AI-related cybersecurity event could fall within A without meeting B's severe-consequence thresholds, while an AI malfunction meeting B could fall outside A if it does not compromise network or information-system security or the financial entity's services.
verdict.practical_consequence: The same AI-related event could be reportable or accountable under one instrument but not the other, creating potentially different incident classifications and duplicated or dropped reporting/accountability responsibilities depending on whether the cybersecurity or severe-impact definition applies.

verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A concerns a service category—an information-society service by reference to Directive (EU) 2015/1535. verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A covers any unique characteristic or data point of a natural person, enterprise, or legal person. Definition B covers all information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person, including information that may identify them directly or indirectly. Thus, an attribute of an enterprise or legal person may fall within A but not B, while information about a natural person need not be a unique characteristic to fall within B.
verdict.practical_consequence: The same data record concerning a natural person could be treated as an 'attribuut' under A and as 'persoonsgegevens' under B, but the scopes and resulting responsibilities differ; data concerning enterprises or legal persons may be covered by A without receiving the personal-data protections and accountability obligations applicable under B.

verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A describes a content-delivery network: geographically distributed servers used to make digital content and services highly available, accessible, or fast for content and service providers. Definition B describes a public electronic communications network by cross-reference to the European Electronic Communications Code, a broader communications-network category intended for public electronic communications services. verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A covers an actual personal-data security breach involving destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure, or unauthorized access. Definition B covers a near-incident: an event that could have endangered data or service availability, authenticity, integrity, or confidentiality, but was successfully prevented or did not occur. The same attempted intrusion or security event could therefore be a near-incident under Definition B while not being a personal-data breach under Definition A if no unauthorized access or other listed harm actually occurred; conversely, an actual event affecting personal data may fall under A without satisfying B's requirement that the harmful outcome was prevented or did not occur.
verdict.practical_consequence: Potential inconsistent classification and accountability: a prevented attack may trigger near-incident reporting or handling under the NIS2 framework but no GDPR personal-data-breach duties, while an actual personal-data compromise triggers GDPR duties even if it is not a near-incident. This can create different reporting, response, and responsibility consequences for the same underlying security event.

verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A covers an electronic identification means containing personal identification data and used to authenticate a natural person, legal person, or undertaking for access to electronic services. Definition B covers a category of personal data produced by technical processing of a natural person's physical, physiological, or behavioral characteristics that enables or confirms unique identification. A biometric datum may be included in an identification means, but an identification means can also use non-biometric data, and biometric data need not itself be an electronic authentication means.
verdict.practical_consequence: The same authentication arrangement could be an 'identificatiemiddel' under A while only its biometric component is 'biometrische gegevens' under B, triggering different scopes of responsibility and safeguards. Conversely, biometric data held for identification may fall under B without constituting an identification means under A, creating a risk of inconsistent classification or dropped obligations if one definition is applied in place of the other.

verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A covers any undertaking that provides ICT services. verdict.practical_consequence: The same undertaking could be subject to ICT third-party-provider obligations under Definition A while not being an operator under Definition B, or could be an operator under Definition B without being an ICT-service provider. Applying the wrong definition could therefore create inconsistent classification and duplicate or dropped regulatory responsibility.

verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A concerns an “ict-product,” incorporating the definition in Regulation (EU) 2019/881. Definition B concerns a “network and information system,” incorporating the definition in Directive (EU) 2022/2555. These are distinct regulatory concepts: an ICT product is a product placed on or supplied to the market, whereas a network and information system is an operational system or infrastructure. An ICT product may form part of such a system, but the system is not thereby the product itself.
verdict.practical_consequence: The same technology or organization could be subject to different classifications and responsibilities: product-focused obligations may apply to the ICT product, while system/operator or entity-focused obligations may apply to the network and information system. Treating them as interchangeable could create duplicated or dropped responsibility, particularly where a product is integrated into a broader system.

verdict.practical_consequence: The same genomic dataset or activity could be subject to GDPR personal-data obligations, including genetic-data safeguards, when linked to an identifiable person, but treated as non-personal data under the AI Act when it is genuinely non-identifiable. verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A covers any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or sets of personal data, including collection, storage, consultation, use, and disclosure. Definition B covers the data entered into or directly acquired by an AI system and used as the basis for generating output. Input data can be personal data and its entry or acquisition can therefore constitute processing, but the concepts are not coextensive: processing is an activity concerning personal data, while input data is a category of data in an AI-system context.
verdict.practical_consequence: The same AI deployment could be classified as involving GDPR processing because it collects or uses personal data, while the AI Act separately classifies the relevant data as input data. Applying only one definition could omit the corresponding controller/processor or AI-system data-governance responsibility, creating duplicated or dropped accountability rather than a single unified classification.

verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A covers a provider of managed services assisting with activities related to cybersecurity risk management, without requiring that the provider belong to a financial group or primarily serve group financial entities. Definition B covers an intra-group ICT-services undertaking, defined by its corporate affiliation and principal customer base, without requiring that its services concern cybersecurity risk management. A financial-group ICT provider may therefore fall under both definitions, only one, or neither depending on the services and organizational facts.
verdict.practical_consequence: The same undertaking or service arrangement could be classified differently: a group ICT provider delivering cybersecurity risk-management assistance may be subject to managed-security-provider obligations under A and intra-group ICT-provider treatment under B, while a group ICT provider delivering non-cybersecurity ICT services would fall under B but not A. This can create inconsistent allocation or duplication of regulatory responsibility, and potentially leave cybersecurity-specific responsibility outside A where the provider is not principally serving group financial entities.

verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A covers the broad infrastructure and data components constituting a network and information system, including electronic communications networks, interconnected devices performing automated digital-data processing, and the relevant digital data. Definition B covers a machine-based system characterized by autonomy, possible post-deployment adaptation, and generation of outputs from inputs for specified objectives. An AI system may be implemented on or through a network and information system, but most network and information systems are not AI systems.
verdict.practical_consequence: The same deployed AI service could fall within both definitions, but the instruments may assign different duties or scopes: the infrastructure operator could be responsible as a network/information-system entity while the AI provider or deployer is responsible as an AI-system actor. Conversely, ordinary networks, devices, or stored data covered by A would not trigger AI-specific classification or obligations under B, creating potentially different accountability boundaries.

verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A concerns an ICT product, by cross-reference to Regulation (EU) 2019/881. Definition B concerns critical infrastructure, by cross-reference to Directive (EU) 2022/2557. A product is a technological good or component, whereas critical infrastructure concerns infrastructure or assets essential for the provision of essential services. They do not define overlapping roles or scopes merely because both involve ICT or security.

verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A concerns a potential circumstance, event, or action capable of harming or negatively affecting network and information systems, their users, or other persons. Definition B concerns a particular type of use of an AI system—use contrary to its intended purpose—that is reasonably foreseeable from human behavior or interaction with other systems. A foreseeable misuse may create a cyber threat, but cyber threats need not involve AI, misuse, or foreseeability; conversely, reasonably foreseeable AI misuse may have effects outside the cyber-threat scope.
verdict.practical_consequence: The same AI-related incident could be classified as both reasonably foreseeable misuse and cyber threat, but responsibility and risk controls could diverge: an AI provider or deployer may be accountable for foreseeable misuse under Definition B, while a separate cyber-risk actor or process may be responsible for the harmful network or information-system effects under Definition A. Applying only one definition could therefore leave a responsibility gap or produce inconsistent classification.

verdict.mismatch_description: An 'ict-actief' is any software or hardware asset in the network and information systems used by a financial entity. verdict.mismatch_description: Definition A describes risk as a quantified possibility of loss or disruption, combining impact magnitude and likelihood. verdict.practical_consequence: The same cyber situation could be treated as an ICT-related incident requiring incident-related accountability under Definition B, while the resulting possibility and severity/likelihood of loss or disruption are assessed as risk under Definition A. Treating them as interchangeable could duplicate or misallocate responsibility, or leave the underlying risk assessment unaddressed when only the incident is recorded.

verdict.practical_consequence: The same incident could be classified as a large-scale cybersecurity incident under one instrument but not as a serious payment-related operational or security incident under the other, or vice versa, leading to different notification, supervisory, and accountability obligations and potentially duplicated or omitted responsibility.

verdict.concrete_scenario: A cloud-computing service provider established outside the EU appoints an EU-established representative under the instrument containing Definition A, while the same provider processes personal data subject to the GDPR and appoints an EU representative under Definition B. If one person is appointed for both roles, the appointment may appear unified, but the two definitions impose different mandates and accountability scopes; if different persons are appointed, each instrument identifies a different representative for the same provider's EU-facing compliance obligations.
verdict.mismatch_description: Both terms designate an EU-established person or legal entity acting for an entity established outside the EU, but they serve different regulatory mandates. Definition A covers representatives of specified digital-service providers, whereas Definition B covers a representative appointed under GDPR Article 27 by a controller or processor for obligations under the GDPR. They are therefore not the same legal role, even though the roles can overlap for one organization. verdict.concrete_scenario: A cloud-based software provider supplies an online service to a bank. The service is supplied electronically and remotely for the bank’s individual request, so it falls within definition A. It is also a continuously provided ICT/data service through ICT systems to an external user, so it falls within definition B. If the applicable instrument asks whether the provider supplies a regulated “digital service” or an “ICT service,” the same provider and activity may receive different scope consequences because definition A is framed around an information-society service supplied, ordinarily for remuneration, at the individual request of a recipient, while definition B is framed around continuous ICT/data services and expressly includes hardware-related services and excludes traditional analogue telephony.
verdict.mismatch_description: The terms overlap substantially but are not the same legal category. Definition A uses the information-society-service criteria, including ordinary remuneration, electronic and remote delivery, and an individual request by the recipient. Definition B covers continuously delivered digital and data services through ICT systems to internal or external users, expressly including hardware-as-a-service and hardware services and excluding traditional analogue telephone services. They therefore provide competing scope tests for whether a provider’s activity is within the relevant regulated service category, rather than merely classifying different attributes or establishing a genus-species relationship.
verdict.practical_consequence: The differing scope criteria can produce inconsistent regulatory classification: a continuously provided ICT service may fall within definition B without satisfying definition A’s individual-request or remuneration conditions, while some information-society services under A may not be continuous ICT services under B. This can create duplicated or dropped compliance responsibilities at the boundary between the instruments.

verdict.concrete_scenario: A ransomware attack encrypts a company's customer database and makes the related online service unavailable, while also causing unauthorized access to or loss of personal data. Under Definition A, the event is an 'incident' because it endangers the availability of services or the integrity/confidentiality of processed data. Under Definition B, it is a 'personal data breach' only insofar as it causes destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure, or unauthorized access to personal data. The same event therefore requires classification for purposes such as notification and incident-response duties, but the two definitions can produce different scopes: a service-availability outage without a qualifying personal-data impact is an incident under A but not a breach under B.
verdict.mismatch_description: The terms are not the same concept. Definition A is a broad network-and-information-systems security/event concept covering threats to the availability, authenticity, integrity, or confidentiality of data or services. Definition B is specifically a personal-data security-breach concept, requiring a qualifying effect on processed data and applying to personal data in the GDPR context. They overlap for security events affecting personal data, but neither is simply a subset of the other in all respects: A covers service availability and authenticity, while B can cover qualifying personal-data destruction, loss, alteration, disclosure, or access without the broader service-impact framing.
verdict.practical_consequence: The same cyber event may trigger the incident regime under A and the personal-data-breach regime under B, while an event affecting service availability or non-personal data may trigger only A. This can create different reporting, response, and accountability consequences, but it is primarily a deliberate difference in regulatory scope rather than a drafting contradiction.

verdict.concrete_scenario: A provider supplies a one-off or intermittent network-based data-processing service, such as a hosted data-processing operation that is not provided continuously to internal or external users. verdict.mismatch_description: Both terms concern ICT-related services and can cover the same provider activity, but definition A focuses on the service's substantive activities—transmission, storage, retrieval, or processing of data—whereas definition B adds a continuous-service and user-oriented scope condition, expressly includes hardware-as-a-service and hardware services, and excludes traditional analogue telephone services. They are therefore not identical definitions and can produce different scope classifications for the same activity. This is not a subset relationship or an orthogonal attribute: both definitions answer the same practical scope question, namely whether an activity is an ICT service under the relevant instrument.
verdict.practical_consequence: The same provider or activity may be subject to ICT-service obligations under one instrument but not the other, creating inconsistent regulatory classification and potentially duplicated or dropped compliance responsibility where the instruments are applied together.
